messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert Weiss is a 67-year-old school principal who came to treatment nearly a year after a life-threatening car accident that occurred on his drive home from campus. He had been stopped at an intersection after a long school day when he heard shouting from somewhere outside, looked up, and in the next instant another vehicle slammed into the side of his car. What stayed with him was not a clear story he could tell from beginning to end, but shards: the violent impact, the metallic crush, the blast of sound, the sense that time had broken apart. Even now he says he cannot really put what happened into words. Instead, the accident returns as a film that plays over and over, and when it comes back he does not feel as though he is remembering something in the past; he feels as if it is happening again.

In the months afterward, Robert had come to believe that the crash revealed something fundamental and terrible. The world no longer felt basically safe to him but dangerous in a way he had not understood before. He judged himself harshly for having been there at all, thinking that someone else would not have gotten into that situation, and he worried that he had been permanently changed for the worse. Those beliefs seemed to prime him for danger everywhere. Shouting in the hallways at school, a loud noise from a locker bank or the cafeteria, or even seeing cars crumpled after an accident on the local news could seize his attention immediately, as if his mind were already searching for signs that another catastrophe was close. When those cues caught him, the crash replayed with a vivid, sensory force that made him feel trapped back inside the car.

His role as a principal made these encounters hard to avoid. A normal day on campus meant raised voices between students, the sudden clatter of dropped equipment, or the jolt of being called to supervise a chaotic moment. He found himself bracing before entering common areas because he was certain that if things became loud or unruly, something bad might happen. That same sense of threat spread beyond obvious reminders of the collision. If his wife was late getting home or a teacher took longer than expected to answer an urgent message, he quickly assumed there had been an accident or some other disaster. He could not relax even in his own house, and nights became long stretches of listening for sounds, unable to settle into sleep. The more on edge he felt, the more easily a shout, a bang, or roadside crash imagery hooked him and pulled the accident back into the present.

The memories themselves drove much of what happened next. Because they arrived so abruptly and intensely, Robert began avoiding work whenever he could manage it, taking days off, delaying his arrival, and finding reasons not to be in the busiest parts of the school. He told himself he was just trying to stay steady. He also forced himself into a kind of rigid optimism, trying to think only positive thoughts whenever the accident intruded, as though refusing darker thoughts might keep him in control. When that failed and the tension kept building, he ate excessively in the evenings, describing it as one of the few things that could dull him enough to get through the night. Yet each of these efforts left him feeling weaker and less like the capable administrator he had always been, which fed his conviction that he had changed for the worse.

That conviction tightened the whole pattern. Because he saw himself as damaged and the world as unsafe, his constant scanning and inability to relax felt justified to him rather than excessive. But living in that state made him more sleepless, more certain that delays signaled disaster, and more vulnerable to the sensory replay of the crash. The more he stayed away from school, shut out difficult thoughts with forced positivity, and ate to manage distress, the less confidence he had in himself. He began to compare himself bitterly to the version of himself who used to handle emergencies calmly, and to other principals who, in his mind, would not be unraveling this way. Avoiding the school environment also made ordinary campus noise feel less familiar, so that when he did return, shouting and sudden loud sounds struck him as even sharper and more threatening.

By the time he sought help, the problem had become impossible to dismiss. A confrontation between two students in a corridor had escalated into shouting, and Robert froze as if the collision were happening again; later that evening, seeing footage of a highway accident on television set off the same reliving response. He barely slept that night and called in sick the next morning, ashamed and frightened by how small his world had become. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was no longer able to do the job that had defined him for decades and that this broken, hypervigilant version of himself might be permanent. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not simply to feel better, but to believe he can walk into his school, hear ordinary noise, and not be transported back to the moment he thought he was going to die.
